Commentary.Commentary: The players are back onto the field. The conditions have become slightly cloudy. 65 overs scheduled for today and another 90 tomorrow. Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul are the openers and it will be Chris Woakes to start off with the new ball, to Jaiswal. Here we go.
... THIRD INNINGS ...

Tough bowling innings for India but they have got to put that behind. They have got around 3-4 overs to negotiate before Lunch and weather and light permitting, 5 sessions to bat and save this Test. Nothing is impossible, but it is highly unlikely that they can make England bat again, but if they can make the hosts toil hard for 100 overs or more, they will be equally tired ahead of the 5th Test. In what came as a surprise, Jasprit Bumrah could not quite strike with the new ball, first or second and that hampered the bowling unit. And Gill's lack of confidence on Shardul Thakur and Washington Sundar helped push the game away to a point from where there was no return. Sundar bowled really well and could have had a bigger say, had he brought on earlier.

For England, it was all about Stokes and his century. And his hamstring. He was seen stretching his hamstring while batting today but they will hope that he can soldier on for one more bowling effort and help his side seal the series. He finally got a Test hundred after 2 years and just exploded after that, scoring a magnificent 141. The innings was otherwise studded by a brilliant 150 by Joe Root, who went past quite a few milestones on Day 3, but not to forget the top 3, who were extremely attacking and took India by the horns. 3 half centuries and 2 centuries really make a good reading as England piled on the highest total at this venue.

The visitors were not at their best with the ball this morning, with the field set being pretty defensive and the body language also, equally sluggish. One can understand that, because after a punishing Day 3, they had their backs against the wall and would only be looking at when would they get to bat. They conceded 125 runs in 22.1 overs, and really struggled to pick up those last 3 wickets. Only Jasprit Bumrah looked to be on song, as he tested the batters while Jadeja managed to get some wickets towards the end.

Excellent batting effort by England but half an hour too late in declaring? Not quite sure what was going through Ben Stokes' mind, despite getting that lead to a position where it is highly unlikely that they will bat again, but still continuing to bat on. Irrespective, the hosts will have around 13 minutes to bowl at India before Lunch, which might see around 3 overs bowled.

ENGLAND END AT 669 AND LEAD BY 311!

Commentary.Commentary: Dark, ominous clouds welcome the players and the umpires back onto the ground. We will definitely have a start on time, but the forecast suggests that it could be a start-stop day for the sport. No overnight declaration, which means that Ben Stokes and Liam Dawson will walk back out with bats in hand, with the major eye on how many overs would the team be comfortable of bowling against India. With due respect, the chances of an Indian win look out of the window but having done so well, if the series goes to The Oval as 2-1, England will feel that they lost a massive opportunity. As expected, it will be Jasprit Bumrah to kick things off. Ben Stokes to face. Let's play!

PITCH REPORT - Deep Dasgupta is pitchside and gives us a detailed look at the surface. He begins by pointing out the overcast skies, saying the Manchester weather has been typically unpredictable this morning. The cloud cover might assist the seamers early on, especially with the new ball on offer. Talking about the pitch itself, he mentions there's still some grass left near the Jimmy Anderson End, and because of that, some cracks have started to appear, which could offer variable bounce and movement for the seamers. Reckons that extra bounce from that end could keep the batters on their toes. At the other Brian Statham end, though, there's visibly less grass, and the surface is already beginning to open up, especially around that good-length region. That’s where it could get tricky for batters, as some balls might keep low and skid on unexpectedly. Deep wraps up by saying it won’t be easy for India if they are made to bat for three or four sessions across Day 4 and Day 5. The surface is only going to get tougher, and with the weather playing its own game, survival won’t be straightforward.

Joe Root, a legend of the game, is up for a quick chat before the start of play. Talking about breaking records and going second on the list of all-time run-scorers in Test cricket, he says it’s been a very cool experience to share the list with legends of the game, the kind of cricketers he grew up idolising. Adds that he used to spend hours, trying to copy their techniques, and as a 10-year-old, he had never believed that he would be standing beside them one day. Speaking about the series, Root calls it massive and reflects on how special yesterday was, especially with the challenge of adapting to the conditions. Mentions that it’s been incredible to play here, referring to the venue and the occasion. Recalls how Sachin Tendulkar made his debut long before him, and yet they ended up playing together in Root’s debut match, something he still finds extraordinary, and adds that he’s always been an inspiration for him. Looking ahead, Root hopes that the weather holds up and notes that the pitch might deteriorate as the match progresses. Ends by saying that yesterday we saw the ball keeping a bit low and there was some steepling bounce as well, so it’ll be interesting how it plays today.

The weather is set to play a big hand. There has been rain in the morning, and the match start is expected under overcast skies, but the bigger concern is Sunday, which carries a high chance of rain. That makes today doubly important, not just for results but for narrative control. Also, it’s the weekend, so the crowd is expected to be buzzing right from the first session itself. Stay tuned for more updates!

As for England, it has been their most complete day in the series. The top order delivered runs, Root turned vintage again, and Stokes showed fight and leadership, returning from cramps late to bat again, while Dawson hung in at the end. But the real question now is how they approach this morning. Can they bat the whole first session and push the lead close to 300? Or, with Sunday’s rain forecast, could we even see some 'Bazballing'? But the longer they bat, the fewer overs they’ll get to bowl India out again. Tactical calls await.

Talking about India first, there’s a lot to introspect. Their bowling attack, which has been consistently potent overseas for close to a decade, finally looked worn. Jasprit Bumrah still led with heart and control, but others leaked runs, and Mohammed Siraj looked fatigued. The captaincy of Shubman Gill will come under the scanner for some tactical delays, especially with the use of spin. Injuries didn’t help either, from Bumrah slipping on the stairs to Siraj cramping up, hampering India’s second-half plans. Still, they’ll have to look to wrap England up quickly in the first session of Day 4, ideally under a 210 lead, and bat long in their second innings to salvage a draw and keep their pride intact.

Let’s rewind the match flow so far. India, after being sent in to bat, posted 358 on the back of steady contributions from Yashasvi Jaiswal, Sai Sudharsan, and Rishabh Pant. England, in reply, began with a bang. Zak Crawley and Ben Duckett stitched a 166-run opening stand, and that momentum rarely dipped. Day 2 ended with England at 225/2, and Day 3 was all about their domination. Joe Root produced a knock of pure class, notching up 150 and surpassing giants like Ricky Ponting, Rahul Dravid, and Jacques Kallis to become the second-highest run-scorer in Test history, only to be behind Sachin Tendulkar. Ollie Pope and Ben Stokes chipped in as well, while India struggled for penetration on a flat but slowish deck. The surface offered occasional uneven bounce, but nothing consistently threatening to trouble batters.

Hello and welcome to all of you for Day 4 of the Fourth Test between England and India from Old Trafford, Manchester. After three absorbing days of cricket, England find themselves in a position of strength, leading by 186 runs with three wickets still intact. For India, despite flashes of resistance with the bat and the ball, they’ve spent a lot of time under pressure. Day 4 arrives with plenty at stake, not just for this match, but also for the momentum heading into the final Test. And with the forecast looming as a character in this drama, it’s going to be a crucial day of play.
... DAY 4, SESSION 1 ...

Which is why, building on the previous paragraph, we should always look ahead, as there is no point in looking back. Unless something miraculous happens, given England's position, it has nearly taken two results out of the game - a tie and an Indian win. But there will be brownie points for psychological advantage. The series has not ended. Neither has the match. If India can come out and bundle the hosts quickly, inside the first 30-45 minutes on Day 4, they can keep England's lead to around 200-210 and try and bat long and hard into the third innings, to carry that form into the 5th Test. Also, Jonathan Trott on air informs us that the forecast is for cloudy weather on Saturday and a major part of Sunday is predicted to be rainy. So, if India can take this game into Day 5, we could have the same result as the 4th Ashes Test in 2023. So, all is not gloomy right now. What about England? How long do they think they need to bat? Will they keep Sunday's weather forecast in mind? An overnight declaration perhaps? All these questions will be answered come Saturday, 26th July, 2025, when Day 4 commences. The first ball is scheduled to be bowled at 3.30 pm IST (1000 GMT), weather and light permitting, but our buildup will begin well in advance. Do tune in early then. ADIOS! TAKE CARE!

Tough day for India. For the first time in nearly a decade, they have conceded a total in excess of 500 away from home. Their bowling attack has been that good over the years. But here, on a track which just looks flat barring inconsistent bounce, their bowlers were put to the sword. Amongst 4 seamers, only Jasprit Bumrah had an economy of under 4. That speaks volumes of his greatness and it is in such times of adversity that everything gets questioned. Could India have selected Prasidh Krishna for this match? Or, with the track supporting spin, could an extra spinner in Kuldeep Yadav have served better than Shardul Thakur? Additionally, why was Washington Sundar not given the ball till the 69th over? And when he and Ravindra Jadeja were bowling in good rhythm, troubling Stokes, why were they taken off the attack just because the second new ball was due? These are questions which the young captain Shubman Gill will have to answer but there are plenty of learnings as well. Such questions pop up only when the team is in trouble.

One hour post the Tea break, things started to happen. For both sides. It started with India, with Bumrah slipping on the stairs while coming out from the dressing room and hurting his ankle and then, Mohammed Siraj getting tired and suffering from cramps as well. It spread to the opposition as Ben Stokes suffered from a stroke of cramps and walked off the field, retired hurt. That led to a flurry of wickets, as England slipped from 491/4 to 528/7, with Root suffering from cramps as well. However, just as the tourists seeked to end the day on a high, Stokes came back again and thwarted them.

The day began with India needing quick wickets to come back into the match but Ollie Pope and Root just denied that. A wicketless morning session ensued and the hosts just kept getting stronger and stronger. Arguably, they got the better of the batting conditions as the sun has been out in full glory throughout this innings. Pope fell for 71 after Lunch, having added a magnificent 144 for the third wicket with Root. This was just when the second new ball was about to be due and all of a sudden, Harry Brook got dismissed as well. India sensed an opportunity but the second new ball did not yield results and Root got into another partnership, this time with Stokes, which yielded 142.

Terrific day for England. Probably, their first since the final day of the first Test in this series, where they have bossed an entire day. The prediction was that if the hosts batted the day out, they will get close to 500 and that's exactly what has happened. In fact, they have reached close to 550. 319 runs came in the day, in 89 overs, for 5 wickets. The wickets fell in clusters, with the first two falling immediately after Lunch and the last 3 falling in the last hour of play. But for a major portion of the day, Joe Root dictated terms, scoring just his second century at this ground in Tests, also his second 150 at this venue as well, holding one end firm. On the way, he went past a few other records, with the most notable among them being jumping to second in the all-time list of run getters in Test cricket.

The scorecard does not paint the true picture. You look and say, yes, 491/4 became 528/7, but what's the big deal? Isn't the lead significant enough? And how much did Stokes add with Dawson on return? Just 11 in a stand of 16, right? Statistically speaking, all the numbers are correct. But, when Chris Woakes was dismissed, there were still around 6 overs left for the day and if Stokes was not going to bat, India needed just 2 more wickets to wrap the innings up. Also, the visitors had gained some momentum after Stokes went off retired hurt, as they conceded only 37 runs in 13.1 overs and picked up 3 quick wickets. For the second time in the day, they had gained some momentum and were on track to end the day on a high, but Mr. Midas stood in their way.

The Old Trafford crowd stands up as one to applaud its Midas. Of course, the day has belonged to Joe Root but Ben Stokes has played a significant part in it. It would have been logical and understandable for him to take the rest of the day off and come back afresh on Day 4, but seeing his side in trouble and sensing that India were on track to bowl England out on Day 3 itself, back he came, hobbling across and like a true champion, saw off the Indians. Take a bow, skip.

... DAY 3, FINAL SESSION ...

Talking about Stokes' struggles, again, Gill's captaincy comes into scrutiny. It is understandable that the second new ball needed to be taken but he could have delayed it for a while. Washington Sundar was bowling beautifully while Jadeja had Stokes dancing up and down. But both got off the attack and the big Ben got off the hook. Having said all of these, Gill is still in his infancy as a captain and will learn with experience.

Day 3 was supposed to be a batting day. Joe Root has literally stamped his authority on that. England have scored 208 runs, of which, Root has scored 110. He has been the cog of the wheel for the home side and has gone past a few records. Climbed up the ladder of most runs in Test cricket and also 50-plus scores. England were in some trouble when Pope and Brook got dismissed in quick succession but Root held his calm. He had the 'nervous 98s' where he spent around 10 balls for 1 run, but that was just a blip in his concentration. Not to forget the contribution of Stokes. He struggled initially, but then, got into his groove and is looking set out there now.

101/2 in 28 overs read England's returns from the session. The Indians picked up both those wickets in the first 37 balls of the session, through Washington Sundar, as he got rid of Ollie Pope and Harry Brook. But unfortunately for Sundar, these wickets came with the second new ball around the corner and got taken off the attack because of that. The point still rings loud - why wasn't Sundar given the ball for 68 overs? The moment he went off the attack, India struggled to find any rhythm and things became worse with Bumrah and Siraj suffering niggles. Kamboj has been decent in patches but raises another question - why wasn't Prasidh Krishna not selected for this game?

The Old Trafford crowd rises as one, to applaud one of England's greatest batters ever and one of the world's greatest too. His skipper has a big smile on his face as he knows that one more good session and the visitors could be shut out of this match. There was just a little bit of stutter en route Root's century, but he has just showed his class.

Commentary.Commentary: It was bright and sunny when the players went for Lunch. It is still bright and sunny when the players are back from Lunch. The sun has kept the clouds at bay, maybe requesting them to come back when the third innings begins. It has been that that kind of a match. Bazball post Lunch? Somehow, get the feeling that England are not going to play traditional cricket for long. They have gone back to the tried and tested methods of playing conservative yet positive cricket in this series, except for the start of this innings. Root and Pope are amidst a fabulous partnership but with the pitch dying down ever so quickly, you can't help but feel that there is that one ball which has got the batter's name on it. Hence, one can never rule out a collapse. Hence, maybe, if the batters try to attack the bowlers, the latter might just lose their lines and lengths and a lead of anything more than 60 could be significant on this deck. Just a reminder, we are yet to see a centurion in this match.

If any, one might just question Gill's line of thought. It is very understandable that India need wickets and hence, the focus is primarily on Jasprit Bumrah and Mohammed Siraj. It is also agreeable that Anshul Kamboj comes in on the back of a heroic 10-wicket haul in a Ranji innings and hence, has been given more overs as the X factor. But in 74 overs, Shardul Thakur has bowled just 6 overs while Washington Sundar was overlooked largely till the 69th over. It is not like India are bowling badly but if the resources are managed slightly better, the main quicks can get more rest. And it is not as if Shardul and Sundar are your part-time options either.

Shubman Gill tried everything he could but with little success, while Jasprit Bumrah maintained tight lines without posing significant threats. India’s fielding was a touch sloppy in this session, and they can’t afford to let chances slip as the longer this partnership continues, the greater the risk of England building a massive lead and potentially batting just once in this Test. The spinners too struggled to make an impact, but with the second new ball due in six overs, the tourists will hope to strike early in the next session and swing the momentum back. The post-Lunch session is scheduled to begin at 6.10 pm IST (1240 GMT).

Ollie Pope and Joe Root were outstanding, batting with intent and punishing anything loose. Both brought up well-crafted fifties and extended their stand to 135 runs to firmly put England in command. Although they had a few nervy moments with some half-chances, a run out looked the most probable way of breaking the partnership as they kept the fielders busy with sharp running. Root, meanwhile, achieved a couple of major milestones in this session, becoming the first batter to score over 1000 Test runs at Old Trafford and moving up to third on the all-time Test run-scorers' list.

SESSION SUMMARY - 107 runs and 0 wickets in 28 overs! England stamped their authority in the opening session, cruising through without losing a wicket and narrowing the deficit significantly. While India showed some improvement with the ball compared to Day 2, the batting-friendly conditions offered little assistance, making it hard for them to create pressure. As a result, the visitors now find themselves leading by just 26 runs and struggling to get back into the contest.

Shardul Thakur of India shares a few words. He says that when they saw there was some movement, they tried to swing the ball from the stumps, but it didn't work. Adds that the English batters kept finding the boundaries even in the tight overs. Says that it was risk and reward game and if they continue to take risks, it might go in India's favour and they can get the breakthroughs.

PITCH REPORT - Deep Dasgupta is pitchside. He says that the conditions look nice and bright, and he expects it to be good for batting. Adds that there is not much of a difference from Day 2, but there will be some variable bounce from the James Anderson end. Mentions that there are a few cracks, and as the sun bakes them, they will start to open up even more.

Anshul Kamboj, the debutant is up for a quick chat. He says that he tried to put extra effort in his first two spells but then backed his strengths in the third one. Adds that there was some movement in the first two days, but then the sun came out and the conditions changed. Says he then tried to hit the right areas and was happy to get his first Test wicket. Ends by saying that England batters are looking to score boundaries, so they have to build pressure with dot balls and create opportunities early on Day 3.

India find themselves in a challenging position after a lackluster bowling effort, managing to claim just two wickets so far, with debutant Anshul Kamboj grabbing his maiden Test scalp as the only real positive. Adding to their woes, the lower order once again failed to contribute, a recurring issue in this series that could prove decisive. With a chance to regroup overnight, the Men in Blue will look to come out with renewed intent, and much will hinge on Jasprit Bumrah’s ability to deliver early breakthroughs, though he’ll need solid support from the rest of the attack. Stay tuned as the action is not far away.

Despite Rishabh Pant’s incredible grit, battling a toe fracture to score a valiant half-century on virtually one foot, Day 2 belonged to England with both bat and ball. Ben Stokes stole the show with a brilliant five-wicket haul, ably supported by Jofra Archer’s incisive spells. The hosts then asserted complete dominance as their openers put on a commanding 166-run stand, although both fell agonizingly short of centuries. Now, with Ollie Pope and Joe Root at the crease, the onus is on them to extend the lead and push India further on the back foot.

Hello and a warm welcome, folks! We’re all set for a crucial Day 3, often called the ‘Moving Day,’ in this 4th Test between England and India. The hosts hold the upper hand, having trimmed the deficit to just 133 runs with 8 wickets still in hand, and given their confident batting display, they’ll be aiming to build a strong lead. On the other hand, India will be desperate for a much-improved effort with the ball to claw their way back into the contest.
... DAY 3, SESSION 1 ...

England, on the other hand, will aim to bat through the day. If they bat the whole of Friday, they will get somewhere between 450-500 which will lend a handy lead in excess of 100. Neither of Ollie Pope or Joe Root looked confident in each's short stay at the crease on Thursday but every day is a new day. The first hour, as always, will be very crucial. If India manage to bowl the hosts out in a couple of sessions, this will become another one-inning shootout. And that will mean, that the hosts will have to bat last on a tricky pitch. In the 6 sessions so far, both teams have won 3 apiece. India won the opening day while England fought back to take the second. Who will take the honours on Day 3 and move the game forward decisively? The first ball will be bowled on Friday, 25th July, 2025, at 3.30 pm IST (1000 GMT) but our buildup will begin well in advance. Also, the weather could be key as well. Join us early then, for all the updates. ADIOS! TAKE CARE!

At the start of Day 2, KL Rahul had mentioned that this is probably the best pitch of the series for batters. Looking at the way England have batted so far, it is very hard to disagree with him. However, the signs of inconsistent bounce are getting bigger and with the sun coming out on Day 2, the pitch might start to break up. That will help the cracks to open up. A day's rest will do good to the Indian bowlers who will come out and concentrate primarily on their lines. They came back well in the final hour, but the lack of control in the two-and-a-half hours prior to that, hurt them. They will start afresh come Friday and look to run through the middle order.

India were all over their lines in the mini session and one expected them to come back harder post Tea. The lines did improve but the result did not vary. The openers continued their run fest and with the Dukes ball getting older and softer, all the bowlers struggled to make it move. Eventually, Ravindra Jadeja managed to get a wicket off a mistake by Crawley, having him caught at first slip for 84, breaking the 166-run stand. That seemed to lift the Indian spirits as the bowling seemed to get better. Debutant Anshul Kamboj did much better in his second spell and managed to get his maiden Test wicket by having Duckett caught behind, for a wonderful 94. The bowling was good in the last hour of play but that blazing opening stand has moved this game quickly at the rate of knotts.

The story completely changed once England came out to bat. Out of nowhere, the dark clouds disappeared and the sun came out in full glory. Add to it, that little shower before Lunch made the ball come nicely onto the bat and the deck seemed totally different from what we had seen during the Indian innings. And on flat tracks, Bazball rarely misses to make its mark. Ben Duckett and Zak Crawley took India by the horns and raced off to around 5 an over. Having required to play around 70 minutes till Tea, they just scored boundaries at will, reaching 77/0 in just 14 overs at the break.

The day began with a big question mark for India. There was no clarity over Rishabh Pant's batting and Ravindra Jadeja was supposed to be their key with the bat. However, he fell in the second over of the day, raising England's hopes of bowling out the visitors under 300. But Shardul Thakur played a valuable hand with Washington Sundar and then, Pant came out bravely to score a few crucial runs to take the visitors beyond 350. At that stage, the weather was murky and some rain had even started to fall once the last Indian wicket fell. Hence, 358 looked like a very big score on this deck.

148/2 in 32 overs in the final session. No doubt as to who won that phase. This has been a solid reply from England and in fact, post the first session on Day 2, it has been all England. In less than 50 overs, they have knocked off more than 60 percent of India's total and the only disappointment for them would be the missing of the centuries by both of their openers.

Commentary.Commentary: The Indians get into a huddle. The dark clouds have disappeared for now and we have got bright sunshine in Manchester. The huddle disperses and the Indians charge onto the field. Back walk the umpires and the opening pair of Duckett and Crawley. Seems like it will be Shardul Thakur to start things off post Tea. Indeed. Crawley to face. 41 overs left in the day, so this will easily be a 150-minute session, weather and light permitting.

Right. We have had 5 sessions and it has been nothing short of a boxing bout. India punching, England counterpunching, India fighting back and so on. The two days have nearly mirrored each other so far. On Day 1, India started well, England fought back, before the visitors took the honours for the day with a fine final session. So far, Day 2's morning session has gone to India, while the hosts have punched back hard in the afternoon. Will the final session, just like Day 1, go in the tourists' favour?
... DAY 2, FINAL SESSION ...

The Indian bowlers weren’t able to exert any real pressure. Jasprit Bumrah bowled tightly early on but was a bit too straight at times and got clipped for boundaries. Mohammed Siraj came in as a first-change and looked sharp, beating the bat and getting some good bounce, but he too couldn't break through with even a review where Crawley got away due to an extra bounce. The debutant Anshul Kamboj seemed to be nervous, leaking runs and struggling with his line. The final session of Day 2 promises more action. England are 77/0 and trail by 281 runs, but with the way they are scoring, they could wipe off that deficit fast. There’s still plenty of time in the match, and with the pitch still looking decent, England will want to bat big. India, meanwhile, will have to regroup quickly during the Tea break. Join us at 8.32 pm IST (3.02 pm GMT) for the final session!

England’s openers then came out all guns blazing. Ben Duckett looked in great touch and played aggressively from the start, putting away anything remotely loose. Zak Crawley, on the other hand, looked a little tentative to begin with but slowly found his timing and started stroking the ball nicely. The duo put on 50 inside 11 overs and didn’t let the Indian bowlers settle. Duckett punished anything on the pads, and there seemed to be a clear plan from India to bowl straight to him, but they conceded too many there. Crawley, despite the pressure of keeping his spot in the playing XI, has started to look more confident as the session progressed. It was the kind of start England needed.

From India’s point of view, it was a disappointing collapse after a promising first half of the innings. Rishabh Pant, who had retired hurt earlier, came back to reach a gutsy half-century. Pant was clearly hampered by his injury and chose to go aerial rather than run. Sundar too got out playing a pull shot to deep fine leg, like Sai Sudharsan earlier. The tail offered very little resistance and collapsed quickly under pressure. India will be a little frustrated not to reach at least the 400-mark after the start they had, especially considering how many batters got starts but none could kick on to get a big hundred.

SESSION SUMMARY - 114 runs, 4 wickets, 23.1 overs. England absolutely dominated the second session, making it their own after an even start to the day. India went into Lunch at 321/6 and would have hoped to stretch their total close to 400. But England’s bowlers had other plans. The session got extended slightly, 10 minutes longer due to an early Lunch. Ben Stokes, the England captain, led the charge with the ball and completed his five-wicket haul in a fiery spell, while Jofra Archer also chipped in with crucial wickets. India were bowled out for 358 in the first hour after the break, losing their last five wickets for just 44 runs.
